Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Who among these is a physicist?
Pick the chemist from these four.
Primo Levi is a chemist. Primo Michele Levi (Italian: [ˈpriːmo ˈlɛːvi]; 31 July 1919 – 11 April 1987) was a Jewish Italian chemist, partisan, Holocaust survivor and writer.
What is the atomic number of Copernicium?
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.
What is the atomic number of Thallium?
Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.
In what year did Johann Wolfgang von Goethe die?
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (28 August 1749 – 22 March 1832) was a German polymath who is widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language.
In what year was Nitrogen discovered?
Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Which company manufactures Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk?
Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk: Skunk Works. It was the first operational aircraft to be designed with stealth technology.
In which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21 based?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: Soviet Union. Approximately 60 countries across four continents have flown the MiG-21, and it still serves many nations seven decades after its maiden flight.
Who is credited with discovering Triangulum Australe?
Triangulum Australe: Américo Vespucio. Triangulum Australe is a small constellation in the far Southern Celestial Hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Ichthyosaurus?
Ichthyosaurus: Mary Anning. It is among the best known ichthyosaur genera, as it is the type genus of the order Ichthyosauria.
Who is credited with discovering Theobroma cacao?
Theobroma cacao: Christopher Columbus. Theobroma cacao (cacao tree or cocoa tree) is a small (6–12 m (20–39 ft) tall) evergreen tree in the Malvaceae family.
Who is credited with discovering Krypton?
Krypton: William Ramsay. Krypton (from Ancient Greek: κρυπτός, romanized: kryptos 'the hidden one') is a chemical element; it has symbol Kr and atomic number 36.
This Swiss chemist discovered the structure of chitin in 1929 and decades later authored a memoir titled 'LSD: My Problem Child' — who was he?
Albert Hofmann (11 January 1906 - 29 April 2008) was a Swiss chemist known for being the first to synthesize, ingest, and learn of the psychedelic effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD).
Closely related to Hepatica and Pulsatilla, which flowering plant genus in the buttercup family is nicknamed the windflower?
Anemone is a genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.
Sharing chemistry with phosphorus and antimony, this group-15 metalloid carries the symbol As and a notorious reputation for toxicity — what is it?
Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
These nocturnal blood-feeding insects from the genus Cimex can trigger skin rashes, itching, and even psychological distress from their bites — what are they commonly called?
Bed bug are insects from the genus Cimex, which are parasites that feed on blood, usually at night.

Native to eastern North America with resident populations as far north as Newfoundland, this crested songbird in the crow family has a black, U-shaped collar around its neck and a mostly white chest — name it?
Blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.
This condition results from inflamed, fluid-filled sacs that cushion friction points between bones, tendons, and muscles, commonly striking the shoulder, elbow, hip, or knee — what is it?
Bursitis is the inflammation of one or more bursae in the body.
Named for its habit of burrowing nests into dead wood or bamboo, this genus of some 500 bee species includes one soil-tunneling exception among its 31 subgenera — what insect is it?
Carpenter bee are species in the genus Xylocopa of the subfamily Xylocopinae.
This class of jawed fish — including sharks and rays — has a skeleton made almost entirely of cartilage, setting it apart from its bony-skeletoned relatives. What class is this?

Chondrichthyes (from Ancient Greek (khndros) 'cartilage' and (ikhths) 'fish') is a class of jawed fish that contains the cartilaginous fish or chondrichthyans, which all have skeletons primarily composed of cartilage.
Named for its snake-like neck (its species epithet means 'snake'), this feisty freshwater reptile has powerful beak-like jaws and ranges from Nova Scotia down to Florida — which species is it?
Common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina) is a species of large, freshwater turtles in the family Chelydridae.
This transdisciplinary field studies circular causal processes like feedback and recursion, where an action's outcome becomes the input for the next — what field is it?
Cybernetics is the transdisciplinary study of circular causal processes such as feedback and recursion, where the outcomes of actions return as inputs for subsequent actions.

This gut ailment flares up when small pouches in the wall of the large intestine become inflamed, often striking with sudden lower-abdominal pain — fever or bloody stool warns of a complication; what is it?
Diverticulitis is a gastrointestinal disease characterized by inflammation of abnormal pouches - diverticula - that can develop in the wall of the large intestine.
Working with George de Hevesy, this Hungarian chemist theorized that diffusion speed depends on a nuclide's mass and became the world's go-to expert at preparing polonium — who was she?
Elizabeth Rona (20 March 1890 - 27 July 1981) was a Hungarian nuclear chemist, known for her work with radioactive isotopes.

The telltale earth mounds this tunneling mammal pushes to the surface come from its constantly expanding burrow system, and it feeds mainly on earthworms paralyzed by toxins in its saliva — what animal is it?
European mole (Talpa europaea) is a mammal of the order Eulipotyphla.
Holding doctorates in both medicine and philosophy from Pisa by age 21, this Italian naturalist became the "founder of experimental biology" by disproving spontaneous generation — who was he?
Francesco Redi (18 February 1626 - 1 March 1697) was an Italian physician, naturalist, biologist, and poet.
This flowering plant genus, whose name derives from the Latin word for a small sword, belongs to the iris family and is centered on the Cape Floristic Region of South Africa — which genus?
Gladiolus (from Latin, the diminutive of gladius, a sword) is a genus of perennial cormous flowering plants in the iris family (Iridaceae).

This British businessman and adventurer, chairman of a Dubai-based aircraft brokerage, visited the South Pole multiple times and descended to the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep before dying in 2023 when a submersible imploded in the North Atlantic - name him?
Hamish Harding (24 June 1964 - 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Domesticated in Central Asia around 4000 BCE, this one-toed hoofed mammal evolved over 45 million years from the small, multi-toed Eohippus — what is it?
Horse (Equus ferus caballus) is a domesticated, one-toed, hoofed mammal.
Found in two forms — a grassland dweller and a darker scrubland cousin — this East and Southern African antelope's scientific name means 'black-footed high-horn.' Which animal?
Impala (Aepyceros melampus, lit. 'black-footed high-horn' in Ancient Greek) is a medium-sized antelope found in eastern and southern Africa.

This Swiss psychologist's theory of cognitive development, paired with his epistemological views, is together known as genetic epistemology, and remains foundational in early-childhood education. Who is he?
Jean Piaget (9 August 1896 - 16 September 1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
This Afghan-American author sought asylum in the U.S. as a teenager and later wrote a bestselling debut novel set in his homeland before working as a UNHCR goodwill ambassador — who is he?
Khaled Hosseini (Pashto/; born March 4, 1965) is an Afghan and American novelist, UNHCR goodwill ambassador, and former physician.
Sometimes a side effect of medication or an alcohol interaction, which state of sluggishness and low motivation usually resolves with rest and better nutrition?
Lethargy is a state of physical or mental weariness, fatigue, sluggishness, or lack of energy.
This paired organ, located near the backbone on either side of the heart in most mammals, extracts oxygen from the air and releases carbon dioxide back into it — name the organ?
Lung are the primary organs of the respiratory system in many animals, including humans.
Working on the geometry of Riemann surfaces, this Tehran-born Stanford professor became in 2014 the first woman and first Iranian to win the Fields Medal — who was she?
Maryam Mirzakhani (12 May 1977 - 14 July 2017) was an Iranian mathematician and a professor of mathematics at Stanford University.

Introduced in 1975 and still in production today at two Russian factories, this Soviet-designed helicopter family serves as both a medium twin-turbine transport and, in gunship form, an armed attack aircraft — what's the helicopter?

Mil Mi-17 (NATO reporting name: Hip) is a Soviet-designed Russian military helicopter family introduced in 1975 (Mi-8M), continuing in production as of 2024 at two factories in Russia, in Kazan and Ulan-Ude.

This symbiotic relationship between a fungus and a plant, in which fungal threads interconnect with plant roots at the cellular level, plays a major role in plant nutrition and soil chemistry — what is it called?
Sold in packs needing a desiccant to keep it from absorbing moisture, this seaweed sheet was once used as currency and shrine offerings in Japan — what is it?
Nori is a dried edible seaweed used in Japanese cuisine, usually made from species of the red algae genus Pyropia, including P. yezoensis and P. tenera.

This female reproductive gland produces eggs that travel through the oviduct to the uterus, while also functioning as an endocrine organ that secretes hormones governing the menstrual cycle — what organ is it?
Ovary (from Latin vrium 'egg') is a gonad in the female reproductive system that produces ova; when released, an ovum travels through the oviduct into the uterus.

Classically, one form of this condition wakes you at night with upper abdominal pain that eases when you eat, while another flares up after meals — and a third of older sufferers feel nothing at all. What is it?
Peptic ulcer disease refers to damage of the inner part of the stomach's gastric mucosa (lining of the stomach), the first part of the small intestine, or sometimes the lower esophagus.

Despite its fearsome reputation as a ferocious predator, this South American freshwater fish actually eats a varied diet that includes plant material, making it more omnivore than monster — what fish is it?
Piranha (or) is any of a number of freshwater fish species in the subfamily Serrasalminae, of the family Serrasalmidae, in the order Characiformes.

An Italian chemist and Auschwitz survivor, he wrote a celebrated memoir of his year in the camp and later a book of stories each named for a chemical element, hailed as the best science book ever — who was he?
Primo Levi (31 July 1919 - 11 April 1987) was a Jewish Italian chemist, partisan, Holocaust survivor and writer.
This Indian Air Force pilot became the first Indian ever to travel to space, flying aboard a Soviet Soyuz mission in 1984 — who is he?
Rakesh Sharma (born 13 January 1949) is an Indian cosmonaut and a pilot of the Indian Air Force.
This woody perennial flowering plant, genus Rosa in the family Rosaceae, includes over 300 species and tens of thousands of cultivars, with sharp prickles on many stems — name the flower?
Rose is either a woody perennial flowering plant of the genus Rosa, in the family Rosaceae, or the flower it bears.
This synthetic element, atomic number 106, is so fleeting that only a few atoms exist at a time and decay within minutes — and it's named for an American nuclear chemist; what is it?
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Sg and atomic number 106.
Pythons and boas of this limbless reptile group still carry a tiny pelvic girdle and vestigial leg-stubs near the cloaca, hinting at long-lost legs. What animal is this?
Snake are elongated legless reptiles of the suborder Serpentes.
This group of cartilaginous fish spans eleven families and roughly 220 species, from tiny river-dwellers to giant manta and devil rays — what group of fish is it?
Stingray are a group of rays, a type of cartilaginous fish.

This chalcogen element, chemically similar to selenium and sulfur, is far more abundant in the universe than on Earth because its hydride escaped into space during our planet's formation — which element?
Tellurium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
A nasty complication of this inflamed-throat illness goes by the wonderfully old-fashioned name 'quinsy,' or peritonsillar abscess — what's the underlying condition?
Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils in the upper part of the throat.
Occasionally causing hearing loss or bone marrow suppression as side effects, this IV antibiotic treats MRSA infections and, in oral form, a common gut infection - which drug?
Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic medication used to treat certain bacterial infections.
This evergreen shrub in the nightshade family, native to the Middle East, North Africa, and the Indian subcontinent, is also known as Indian ginseng or winter cherry — what is its scientific name?

Withania somnifera is an evergreen shrub in the Solanaceae family that is native to the Middle East and North Africa, other African regions, southern Europe, Indian subcontinent, and across Southeast Asia.
This bird-of-prey family boasts 256 species including eagles, hawks, kites, and harriers, though the osprey and secretary bird are classified separately — which family is it?
Accipitridae: Family of birds of prey. The Accipitridae have a cosmopolitan distribution, being found on all the world's continents (except Antarctica) and a number of oceanic island groups.
Conceived as a clean-sheet 'extra wide body' answer to Boeing's Dreamliner, this twin-engine jet first lifted off from Toulouse in 2013 on Rolls-Royce Trent power — which airliner is it?
Airbus A350: Large twin-aisle airliner family.
Refined from bauxite and nicknamed alumina, this compound shows up in nature as the mineral corundum — the very stuff of rubies and sapphires. What is it?
Aluminium oxide: Chemical compound. Aluminium oxide (or aluminium(III) oxide) is a chemical compound of aluminium and oxygen with the chemical formula Al2O3.
Named for a 19th-century Swedish physicist and symbolized by a letter of the Swedish alphabet, which unit of length equals one ten-billionth of a metre, handy for measuring atoms and bond lengths?
Angstrom: Unit of length. The unit is named after the Swedish physicist Anders Jonas Ångström (1814–1874).
Nicknamed the 'Primeval Bird' in German, this magpie-sized, feathered dinosaur from 150-million-year-old Jurassic Germany was long hailed as the earliest known bird — what is it?
Archaeopteryx: Extinct genus of bird-like dinosaurs.

This rapid, irregular quivering of the heart's upper chambers can be entirely silent or bring palpitations and fainting — and it sharply raises the risk of stroke, dementia and heart failure. What is this arrhythmia?
Atrial fibrillation: Irregular beating of the atria of the heart.

Nicknamed the 'stone' or 'house' version of its family, this adaptable mustelid outcompetes its forest-specialist, pine-dwelling cousin in open habitats — and has even gone feral in North America. Which species is it?
Beech marten: Species of carnivore. It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List on account of its wide distribution, its large population, and its presence in a number of protected areas.
Predicted by Einstein's general relativity, this astronomical body is so compact that not even light can escape past its event horizon. What is it?
Black hole: Compact astronomical body. A black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping.

This rare and potentially fatal illness comes from a toxin better known by its cosmetic nickname; it starts with blurry vision and slurred speech but usually spares both fever and consciousness — what is it?
First proposed after the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese, this psychological theory says people are less likely to help a victim when others are present — what's it called?
Bystander effect: Social psychological theory. Recent research has focused on "real world" events captured on security cameras, and the coherency and robustness of the effect has come under question.

This polyatomic ion, CO3 with a 2- charge, is dissolved into water under pressure to make it fizzy, and also makes up much of the sedimentary rock in the Earth's crust — what's the ion (and salt) called?
Carbonate: Salt or ester of carbonic acid.
Discovered in 1945 and first sold in 1964, this class of beta-lactam antibiotics was originally pulled from a fungus once known as Cephalosporium — what's the family called?
Made in the skin after sun exposure and also known as vitamin D3, this compound is converted by the liver and kidneys into forms that help the body absorb calcium. What is it?

Cholecalciferol: Vitamin D3, a chemical compound. Cholecalciferol, also known as vitamin D3, colecalciferol or calciol, is a skin-made vitamin D that is found in certain foods and used as a dietary supplement.
This scale insect that feeds on prickly pear cacti produces carminic acid, the basis of the red dye carmine used in lipstick and food coloring — what is it?
Cochineal: Species of insect producing the crimson dye carmine.
Known historically as blue vitriol, this bright blue crystalline compound with the formula CuSO4 forms an octahedral complex when dissolved in water — what compound?
Copper(II) sulfate: Chemical compound. It forms hydrates CuSO4·nH2O, where n can range from 1 to 7.
Sold under trade names like Super Glue and Krazy Glue, this fast-acting adhesive family rapidly polymerizes the moment it contacts water — which chemical group?
Cyanoacrylate: Type of fast-acting adhesive. The cyanoacrylate group in the monomer rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water to form long, strong chains.
With evidence of practice dating back to 7000 BC, this field is considered the very first specialization to branch off from general medicine — what is it?
Dentistry: Branch of medicine. Dentistry, also known as dental medicine and oral medicine, is the branch of medicine focused on the teeth, gums, and mouth.
Nicknamed 'Spad' after a World War I fighter, this piston-engine attack plane flew from 1946 into the 1980s, an anachronism deep into the Jet Age — which aircraft?
Douglas A-1 Skyraider: American single engine attack aircraft.
Linked with orgasm and involving involuntary pelvic-floor contractions, this male bodily process can even happen during sleep as a so-called 'wet dream' — what is it?
Ejaculation: Semen discharge from the male reproductive tract.
This 1939 Nobel Physics laureate invented the cyclotron and went on to found two national laboratories that carry his surname today — who was he?

Scientifically known as Chloris chloris, this small finch is widespread across Europe, North Africa, and Southwest Asia, and has also been introduced to Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Argentina — what bird is this?
European greenfinch: Species of bird. The European greenfinch or simply the greenfinch (Chloris chloris) is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae.
Native to the Mediterranean and grown since ancient times, this teardrop-shaped fruit is technically a syconium and comes from the type species of a genus with over 800 members — what fruit is it?
Fig: Species of flowering plant, or its fruit.
Also called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon or Red Car Theory, this cognitive bias makes you notice something everywhere right after you first learn about it — what is it?
Frequency illusion: Kind of cognitive bias. The name "Baader–Meinhof phenomenon" was coined in 1994 by Terry Mullen in a letter to the St.

Arriving late to a lecture, this mathematician copied down two famous unsolved problems in statistics, mistook them for homework — and solved them; he's better known for inventing the simplex algorithm for linear programming. Who was he?

This German engineer invented the high-speed petroleum engine, working alongside his lifelong partner Wilhelm Maybach to build small, fast motors they hoped to mount on any kind of vehicle. Who was he?
Gottlieb Daimler: German engineer, industrialist and automotive pioneer (1834–1900)
Often translated as 'Jewish law' but literally meaning 'the way of walking,' this body of religious rules draws on the Torah, the Talmud, and codes like the Shulchan Aruch — what is it called?
Halakha: Jewish rabbinical law. Halakha is often translated as "Jewish law", although a more literal translation might be "the way one proceeds" or "the way of walking".
This German-American statistician patented an electromechanical punched-card tabulating machine in 1884, founding a company that would eventually be renamed IBM — who was he?
Herman Hollerith: American statistician and inventor. Hollerith founded a company that was amalgamated in 1911 with several other companies to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company.

This fatal inherited neurodegenerative disorder, once called a 'chorea,' starts with subtle mood changes before bringing on uncoordinated, dance-like involuntary movements as the basal ganglia degrade — what is it?
Huntington's disease: Inherited neurodegenerative disorder. Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.
Roche once used up to 90% of the world's crop of this star-shaped spice to manufacture the flu drug Tamiflu via shikimic acid — what is it?
Illicium verum: Star anise, an evergreen tree.
The largest tree fruit on Earth can hit 120 pounds and 35 inches long — a 'multiple fruit' made of thousands of individual flowers, with a single tree bearing hundreds a year. What is it?
This physician ran the Battle Creek Sanitarium — part spa, part hospital, part luxury hotel — where he treated the rich and poor alike and devised numerous nut and vegetable products — who is it?
Born in Kabul to a diplomat, this Afghan-American physician-turned-novelist wrote the bestselling 'The Kite Runner' before serving as a UNHCR goodwill ambassador — who is he?
Khaled Hosseini: Afghan-American novelist (born 1965). Hosseini's novels have spread awareness about Afghanistan's people and culture.
The last member of the actinide series, this synthetic element honors the man who invented the cyclotron — the very machine used to discover so many artificial elements. Which element is it?
Lawrencium: Chemical element with atomic number 103 (Lr)
Named in honor of a pioneer of sterile surgery, this genus of bacteria causes a rare but serious foodborne illness with a fatality rate up to 30 percent — what is it?
Listeria: Genus of bacteria. Listeria is a genus of bacteria that acts as an intracellular parasite in mammals.
Named from a Greek root meaning 'light' or 'brightness' in reference to its luminous, reflective eyes, this genus includes the bobcat among its four wild cat species — which genus?
Lynx: Genus of medium-sized wild cats.
A Russian pediatric endocrinologist also known by the surname Faassen, this woman is the elder child of Russia's president. Who is she?
Maria Vorontsova: Daughter of Vladimir Putin (born 1985)
This waxy crystalline compound from peppermint and corn mint produces a cooling sensation when inhaled or rubbed on skin, and brings local-anesthetic relief to a sore throat — what is it?
Menthol: Organic compound used as flavouring and analgesic.
Soviet pilots nicknamed this 1972 gunship the 'flying tank,' a helicopter NATO calls 'Hind' that can also haul eight troops and still flies in 52 countries. What is it?
Mil Mi-24: Family of assault and attack helicopters.
Numbering roughly 160,000 species and mostly active at night, these insects share an order with butterflies but are known for their duller, darker wings — what are they?
Moth: Group of mostly-nocturnal insects in the order Lepidoptera.
Also called the belly button, this flat or hollowed spot on the abdomen marks where the umbilical cord once attached — what is it?
Navel: Scarred area on the abdomen after detachment of the umbilical cord.

As the United States' first swept-wing fighter jet, this Korean War-era aircraft dueled Soviet MiG-15s in some of history's earliest jet-to-jet battles — which plane, produced in more than 7,800 units?
North American F-86 Sabre: Family of US fighter aircraft.

The world's most widespread and commercially important cactus species, this domesticated crop is grown both as a fruit and for its edible vegetable pads, likely originating in central Mexico — which species?
Opuntia ficus-indica: Species of cactus. It is grown primarily as a fruit crop, and also for the vegetable nopales and other uses.
One researcher catalogued as many as 549 varieties of this psychological category, defined by intense arousal toward things that aren't sexual by nature — what is the term?
This serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity and serves as a conduit for the blood vessels and nerves of the organs it covers — what is it called?
Peritoneum: Membrane that forms lining of abdominal cavity or coelom.
Domesticated twice in the Neolithic — once near the Tigris Basin and once in China — this even-toed, hoofed omnivore is farmed mainly for pork; what is it?

In this group of disorders, pigment-like substances called porphyrins accumulate in the body, triggering attacks of abdominal pain, confusion, and even seizures that can be set off by alcohol or fasting. What is it?
Porphyria: Metabolic disorders in which porphyrins build up in the body.

Found in more than 200 species of mushroom, this tryptamine alkaloid is itself biologically inactive — the body must dephosphorylate it into psilocin before the euphoria and time-bending kick in. What is it?
Psilocybin: Chemical compound found in some species of mushrooms.
Flying aboard Soyuz T-11 in April 1984 as part of the Soviet Interkosmos programme, who became the first citizen of his country to reach outer space?
Rakesh Sharma: First Indian to travel to space (born 1949)
He shared the 1965 Nobel for quantum electrodynamics and dreamed up a now-famous pictorial shorthand for the behavior of subatomic particles — which physicist lent his name to those diagrams?
About 500 times sweeter than table sugar but prone to a bitter, metallic aftertaste, this odorless artificial sweetener also goes by the additive code E954 — what is it?
Comprising seven species from the flatback to the leatherback, five of these ocean-dwelling reptiles are threatened with extinction — what are they?
Sea turtle: Reptiles of the superfamily Chelonioidea.
Highly water-soluble and non-hygroscopic, this colorless compound with formula AgNO3 is the least expensive salt of its kind — which compound?
Silver nitrate: Chemical compound. It is highly water soluble colorless solid that is a precursor to many other silver compounds.
This healthcare discipline treats disorders of voice, fluency, and swallowing, practiced by clinicians licensed under boards overseen by groups like ASHA — which field of study?
Belonging to a fish family whose fossils date back to the Late Cretaceous, these long-lived, late-maturing fish share their order with paddlefish and once swam as far as North Africa — what are they?
Pig-shaped with a short, flexible snout, this odd-toed ungulate mammal lives in the jungles of South and Central America and Southeast Asia, alongside equine and rhino relatives — which animal?
As head of Harland and Wolff's drafting department, this shipbuilder helped design the Olympic-class liners and went down with the most famous of them on her maiden voyage — who was he?
Thomas Andrews: British businessman and shipbuilder (1873–1912)
Sold as Tramal, this opioid painkiller doubles as an SNRI — which means it carries a rare risk of serotonin syndrome. What is it?
This hypothetical element 126, nicknamed eka-plutonium, intrigues physicists because 126 may be a 'magic number' of protons sitting near the center of a predicted island of stability — what is it?
Unbihexium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 126 (Ubh)
This chronic autoimmune disorder causes patches of skin to lose their pigment, and in antiquity it was so misunderstood that it was often confused with leprosy — what is it?
Vitiligo: Skin condition where patches lose pigment.
A short evergreen shrub with dull green leaves and orange-red berries, this nightshade-family plant is better known by names like Indian ginseng and winter cherry — what is it?
Withania somnifera: Species of flowering plant.
The symbol for silicon is Si. Silicon is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
The symbol for fermium is Fm. Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.
